Unusually for the Austronesian family—although not so unusually for the RASH languages of Raja Ampat [14, 16]—both languages have lexical tone. The tone systems are modest, and specifications are generally culminative and limited to word-final syllables. In Butlih, there is a contrast between High, Rise, and toneless syllables; in Biga, the contrast is between High, Extra-High, and toneless syllables. ... new_statements.quote: [p.13] The word prosodic systems of the Maˈya dialects (Kawe, Laganyan, Wauyai, Salawati, Misool) and Biga are all very similar. [...] all these varieties are analysed with both lexical tone and lexical stress. [...] in Biga it is between High, Extra‑High, and toneless syllables. [p.14] Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties [...] There are no restrictions on which tones may combine with penultimate stress in Biga (e.g. ˈlomo³s ‘blood’ and ‑ˈama³t ‘to burn (intr.)’ with High tone; ‑ˈini⁴m ‘to drink’, kaˈbutu⁴ ‘cold’ with Extra‑High tone), although toneless words with penultimate stress are not attested.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Biga has lexically contrastive stress on either the penultimate or the final syllable of polysyllables (not predictable), combined with a culminative lexical tone contrast (High vs Extra-High vs toneless) restricted to the word-final syllable; stress and tone are independent, giving pairs like ˈmana³ 'light (weight)' vs maˈme³ 'red' (Table 7). Section 1 (p. 2): 'both Maˈya and Biga combine lexical tone with a system of contrastive stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Strong tendency for penultimately stressed words to have identical vowels in the penultimate and final syllables (kaˈmumu³s 'mosquito', ˈbini³s 'hot'); toneless words with penultimate stress are not attested; unlike the Maˈya dialects, no tone restriction on penultimately stressed words; no phrase-medial apocope in Biga; toneless words take optional prepausal epenthetic /-o/. fn. 12: 'The word prosody of Biga is not described elsewhere in the literature.' Phonetic correlates of stress are given only for Salawati Maˈya (duration, vowel quality, intensity; Remijsen 2001a).
new_statements.identity_note: Arnold 2025 describes the Biga language of Biga village, Misool (Raja Ampat), which she treats as an offshoot of Kawe Maˈya within the Waigeo Maˈya branch of Maˈya-Salawati (ms p. 17); no dialect split within Biga is discussed. The stress generalisation on ms p. 14 is stated for 'all varieties' (the five Maˈya dialects and Biga), with Biga-specific examples and Table 7/Table 9 columns; the phonetic-correlate detail is Salawati Maˈya only.

audit.recode_to: classification lexical (contrastive stress, penultimate vs final, unpredictable) + lexical tone (High / Extra-High / toneless, culminative, word-final syllable); edge=right (two-syllable window), domain=word — i.e. code Biga exactly as the catalog already codes Kawe (kawe1240), Wauyai (wauy1237) and Salawati/Misool Ma'ya (maya1282). Deciding source: Arnold 2025, Oceanic Linguistics 64(1):86-144, sec. 4.1 + Table 9 (accepted manuscript pp.13-16, now obtained).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated locators in the copies we hold (ICPhS 2023 sec.1/2.3; Arnold 2020 pp.27-28; Remijsen 2001 pp.139, 158). (2) The tone classification is secure: the fieldworker's own statements (2020 survey, 2021 talk abstract downloaded now, 2023 ICPhS, 2023 ICHL abstract) all describe Biga as lexical-tone (High / Extra-High / toneless, culminative, word-final). But none of the reached sources is a description of Biga word prosody, none says anything about stress, and Glottolog has no grammar/phonology for Biga at all. (3) A clearly better source exists and is not yet obtained: Arnold 2025 OL 64(1):86-144, 59 pp. on tone and stress in the Ma'ya-Salawati languages, paywalled with no open manuscript found (ANU portal, Edinburgh, author site, Crossref all checked). Its abstract reconstructs lexical stress for the proto-language and says several daughters keep

sources.quote: 'I will show that Butlih Salawati, Batta, and Biga all have lexical tone ... the tonal inventory of Biga is highly typologically unusual, in that the unmarked tonal category (tonelessness) is of a lower pitch than the two marked tonal categories (High and Extra-High).' sources.quote: 'the synchronic word-prosodic systems of the daughter languages are ... (i) all tonal ... and (ii) several additionally have contrastive stress ... Proto-Ma'ya-Salawati itself can be reconstructed with both tone and lexical stress ... prosodic developments conditioned by syllable loss.' Biga not named in the abstract.
sources.note: The only dedicated analysis of tone AND stress in the subgroup Biga belongs to, by the sole fieldworker; our record says 'no stress rule stated in any reached source' and codes classification tonal, while Biga's closest relatives (Kawe/Laganyan/Wauyai Ma'ya) are coded classification lexical (contrastive stress + tone) and the abstract says 'several [daughters] additionally have contrastive stress' — this paper settles whether Biga has contrastive stress, predictable (final) stress, or none.

sources.note: Presents Biga (from the author's own fieldnotes) as a tone language with a three-way contrast on (word-final) syllables between High, Extra-High and toneless, exemplified lú 'sea' / lű 'two', Íf 'island' / I̋s 'dog', pít 'moon' / űt 'louse' / put 'thorn'; no stress statement for Biga in this deck (stress is described only for Ma'ya, p.42). The diachrony part argues RA tone is neither coincidence nor Austronesian inheritance but reflects contact with now-extinct tonal Papuan languages.
